title: Private Adaptive Covariance Estimation via Gaussian Graphical Models
topic: Social Aspects->Privacy-preserving Statistics and Machine Learning
claim: Our adaptive method beats standard baselines in estimation error, especially in high dimensions and at low-to-moderate privacy budgets.
layout: 2x5 grid of log-log line plots, columns are datasets, rows are error metrics
description: A 2×5 grid of log-log line plots. Each column is a real dataset, titled with its dimension: adult (d=6), thyroid_ann (d=21), ibm (d=23), bank32nh (d=33) and communities_crime (d=102). The top row plots Mahalanobis error and the bottom row plots Frobenius error. The x-axis is the privacy parameter ρ, running from about 10^-3 to 10^1. Each panel has three lines with markers and shaded bands for variability: PACE-GGM in blue circles, SSP in red squares, and AdaptiveCov in orange diamonds. Errors fall as ρ grows. In the higher-dimensional datasets the blue curve sits well below the red and orange curves at small ρ. The curves converge, or the baselines slightly win, at large ρ. In the adult panel the methods are close, and SSP is better at large ρ. The legend is in the top-left panel.
caption: Budget annealing
abstract: We propose PACE-GGM, a data-adaptive differentially private method for covariance estimation that concentrates its privacy budget on the most informative entries of the empirical covariance matrix, rather than perturbing all entries. This applies in the natural setting where the modeler supplies separate bounds for each variable, so that individual entries can be measured with less noise than the full matrix. In each round, our method selects a poorly approximated entry, measures it using the Gaussian mechanism, and then reconstructs a full covariance matrix using a maximum-entropy reconstruction objective, leading to a Gaussian graphical model structure. Experiments on diverse real-world datasets demonstrate consistent improvements in estimation error with respect to the Gaussian mechanism and other baselines, particularly in high-dimensional and low-to-moderate privacy regimes.
